claim: Mrc1a-positive perivascular cells cover the zebrafish brain at an average density of 2551.25 ± 248.35 S.D. cells per dorsal side of brain in adult zebrafish (n = 4).
source: Although we observe some Mrc1a:eGFP-positive lymphatic vessels around the brain (see below) we also found very large numbers of individual, strongly Mrc1a:eGFP-positive cells covering the surface of much of the adult brain (2551.25 ± 248.35 S.D. cells/dorsal side of brain, n = 4, Figure 1a,b, Figure 1—figure supplement 1).
evidence: The manuscript provides specific quantitative measurements from imaging experiments on n=4 adult zebrafish brains.

claim: Mrc1a-positive perivascular cells are particularly dense on the surface of the optic tectum.
source: These cells are particularly dense on the surface of the optic tectum (Figure 1a,b, Figure 1—figure supplement 1a), but they are also found on the dorsal side of the cerebellum, the ventral side of the hypothalamus and on the olfactory bulbs (Figure 1—figure supplement 1b).
evidence: The claim is supported by confocal imaging data shown in the referenced figures.

claim: Mrc1a-positive perivascular cells are flat, elongated spindle-shaped cells with an average length of 39.46 ± 11.61 S.D. μm (n = 218).
source: High-resolution confocal imaging of individual perivascular cells shows they are flat, elongated spindle-shaped cells 40 μm (39.46 ± 11.61 S.D., n = 218) in length.
evidence: The manuscript provides quantitative morphological measurements from high-resolution confocal imaging of 218 cells.

claim: Mrc1a-positive perivascular cells reside only in the most exterior meningeal layers of the adult zebrafish brain.
source: Cross sections of the adult zebrafish brain confirmed that these perivascular cells reside only in the most exterior meningeal layers (Figure 1e–g).
evidence: The claim is supported by cross-sectional imaging data shown in Figure 1e-g.

claim: Mrc1a-positive perivascular cells are mostly disconnected cells that do not form tubes.
source: Higher magnification confocal imaging shows that these strongly GFP-positive cells are mostly disconnected cells that do not form tubes, although they are found very closely apposed to blood vessels (Figure 1c,d).
evidence: The claim is supported by confocal imaging data shown in Figure 1c,d.

claim: Mrc1a-positive perivascular cells are present on the surface of the brain in developing zebrafish at 10, 15, and 30 dpf.
source: Mrc1a:eGFP-positive perivascular cells are also present on the surface of the brain in developing zebrafish, as can be seen in 10, 15, and 30 dpf animals (Figure 2a–g).
evidence: The claim is supported by imaging data at multiple developmental time points shown in Figure 2a-g.

claim: Mrc1a-positive perivascular cells appear EdU-negative during development, suggesting they are not proliferating on the tectum but arriving from elsewhere.
source: The Mrc1a-positive perivascular cells on the surface of the tectum increase in number over time but appear EdU-negative during development, suggesting they are not proliferating there but arriving from elsewhere (Figure 2—figure supplement 1a).
evidence: The claim is supported by EdU staining experiments shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1a.

claim: Mrc1a-positive brain perivascular cells are also marked by Lyve1:dsRed transgene.
source: Interestingly, Mrc1a:eGFP-positive brain perivascular cells are also marked by several other transgenes known to be expressed in lymphatic or lympho-venous endothelial cells, including Lyve1:dsRed (Figure 2h–j) and Prox1aBAC:KalTA4-4xUAS-E1b:uncTagRFP (from here on called Prox1a:RFP) (Figure 2k–m), suggesting a potential lymphatic lineage relationship.
evidence: The claim is supported by double-transgenic imaging data shown in Figure 2h-j.

claim: Mrc1a-positive brain perivascular cells are also marked by Prox1a:RFP transgene.
source: Interestingly, Mrc1a:eGFP-positive brain perivascular cells are also marked by several other transgenes known to be expressed in lymphatic or lympho-venous endothelial cells, including Lyve1:dsRed (Figure 2h–j) and Prox1aBAC:KalTA4-4xUAS-E1b:uncTagRFP (from here on called Prox1a:RFP) (Figure 2k–m), suggesting a potential lymphatic lineage relationship.
evidence: The claim is supported by double-transgenic imaging data shown in Figure 2k-m.

claim: Mrc1a-GFP-positive cells do not take up intramuscularly injected Q-dots, unlike other lymphatic vessels surrounding the brain.
source: However, Mrc1a-GFP-positive cells are not part of either blood or lymphatic vessels, do not form tubes and, in contrast to other lymphatic vessels surrounding the brain, Mrc1a-GFP-positive cells do not take up intramuscularly injected Q-dots (Figure 2—figure supplement 1b,c).
evidence: The claim is supported by Q-dot injection experiments shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1b,c.

claim: Zebrafish Mrc1a-positive perivascular cells contain numerous large intracellular vesicular/vacuolar compartments that emit weak yellow autofluorescence.
source: Higher magnification confocal imaging of perivascular cells on the brains of Tg(mrc1a:eGFP) or Tg(lyve1:dsRed) adult zebrafish reveals that they contain numerous large intracellular vesicular/vacuolar compartments that emit weak yellow autofluorescence (Figure 3c–f).
evidence: The claim is supported by confocal imaging data shown in Figure 3c-f.

claim: Autofluorescent cells are present in close proximity to blood vessels on the cortical surface of the brain in wildtype, non-transgenic adult zebrafish.
source: Fluorescent imaging of dissected brains from wildtype, non-transgenic adult zebrafish reveals that these cells are in close proximity to blood vessels on the cortical surface of the brain (Figure 3a,b).
evidence: The claim is supported by fluorescent imaging of wildtype zebrafish brains shown in Figure 3a,b.

claim: Mammalian FGPs are strongly positive for MRC1 (CD206).
source: As in the zebrafish, mammalian FGPs are found in the superficial leptomeningeal layers of the brain (Mato and Ookawara, 1979; Mato et al., 1981, 1985), and we find that murine FGPs are also strongly positive for MRC1 (CD206) (Figure 3g,h).
evidence: The claim is supported by immunostaining data on mouse brain sections shown in Figure 3g,h.

claim: India Ink injected into the brains of adult Tg(mrc1a:eGFP) zebrafish is taken up by Mrc1a:eGFP-positive FGPs.
source: India Ink injected into the brains of adult Tg(mrc1a:eGFP) zebrafish is taken up by Mrc1a:eGFP-positive FGPs, as evidenced by the appearance of dark vesicles (Figure 3i,j).
evidence: The claim is supported by India ink injection experiments shown in Figure 3i,j (n = 3/10 injected brains).

claim: Zebrafish FGPs become elongated following an acute high cholesterol diet (HCD).
source: Similarly, zebrafish FGPs become elongated and accumulate a larger amount of lipid droplets following an acute high cholesterol diet (HCD) (Figure 3k–n).
evidence: The claim is supported by quantitative measurements showing statistically significant increase in cell length (T-test, p-value=1.7×10−10, n = 347 FGPs from 3 adult brains) shown in Figure 3k-n.

claim: Zebrafish FGPs accumulate a larger amount of lipid droplets following an acute high cholesterol diet (HCD).
source: Similarly, zebrafish FGPs become elongated and accumulate a larger amount of lipid droplets following an acute high cholesterol diet (HCD) (Figure 3k–n).
evidence: The claim is supported by quantitative measurements showing statistically significant increase in vacuole number (T-test, p-value=9.2×10−6, n = 354 FGPs from 3 adult brains) shown in Figure 3k-n.

claim: Lyve1:dsRed-positive FGPs and Pdgfrb:Citrine-positive pericytes/smooth muscle cells are separate cell populations on the surface of the brain.
source: Confocal imaging of a Tg(lyve1:dsRed);Tg(pdgfrb:Citrine) double-transgenic adult zebrafish shows that although Pdgfrb:Citrine-positive pericytes or vascular smooth muscle cells and Lyve1:DsRed-positive FGPs reside both in close proximity on the surface of the brain, they are separate cell populations (Figure 4b,c), with the FGPs representing a population of larger and more elongated cells.
evidence: The claim is supported by double-transgenic imaging data shown in Figure 4b,c (n = 2 brains imaged).

claim: Mrc1a:eGFP-positive cells are not microglia based on neutral red staining.
source: To address the possibility that Mrc1a:eGFP-positive cells are microglia, we used a neutral red vital dye previously shown to strongly label microglial lysosomes in the zebrafish (Herbomel et al., 2001). Zebrafish larvae exposed to neutral red showed clear labeling of microglia cells on the dorsal brain at 5 dpf, but these were not on the developing optic tectum where the Mrc1a:eGFP-positive FGPs (which were not stained with neutral red) were located (Figure 4d,e).
evidence: The claim is supported by neutral red staining experiments shown in Figure 4d,e (n = 15 animals).

claim: Lyve1:dsRed-positive FGPs do not express Mpx:eGFP.
source: Confocal imaging of Tg(lyve1:dsRed);Tg(mpx:eGFP) or Tg(mrc1a:eGFP);Tg(lyz:dsRed) double transgenic animals also shows that Lyve1:dsRed-positive FGPs do not express Mpx:eGFP, nor do Mrc1a:eGFP-positive FGPs express Lyz:dsRed, and the FGPs are clearly distinct from Mpx:eGFP or Lyz:DsRed-expressing neutrophils (Figure 4f–n).
evidence: The claim is supported by double-transgenic imaging data shown in Figure 4f-n (n = 3 animals imaged).

claim: Mrc1a:eGFP-positive FGPs do not express Lyz:dsRed.
source: Confocal imaging of Tg(lyve1:dsRed);Tg(mpx:eGFP) or Tg(mrc1a:eGFP);Tg(lyz:dsRed) double transgenic animals also shows that Lyve1:dsRed-positive FGPs do not express Mpx:eGFP, nor do Mrc1a:eGFP-positive FGPs express Lyz:dsRed, and the FGPs are clearly distinct from Mpx:eGFP or Lyz:DsRed-expressing neutrophils (Figure 4f–n).
evidence: The claim is supported by double-transgenic imaging data shown in Figure 4f-n (n = 2 animals time-lapse imaged).

claim: Following laser injury to an FGP-containing brain vessel, Lyz:DsRed-positive neutrophils migrate transiently to the wound area and frequently interact with adjacent FGPs.
source: Although few if any Lyz:DsRed-positive neutrophils are normally observed on the brain of 5 dpf developing zebrafish, following laser injury to an FGP-containing brain vessel Lyz:DsRed-positive neutrophils can be observed migrating transiently to the wound area (Figure 4h–n). Interestingly, although the Mrc1a:eGFP-positive FGPs adjacent to the wound do not appear to migrate themselves, the migrating neutrophils frequently appear to physically interact with these FGPs (Figure 4i,k,m,n).
evidence: The claim is supported by time-lapse imaging data following laser injury shown in Figure 4h-n.

claim: Mrc1a-eGFP(+) FGPs and Mpeg1-mCherry(+) macrophages are distinct cell populations at 5 dpf and 15 dpf.
source: Confocal imaging of 5 dpf or 15 dpf old Tg(mrc1a:eGFP); Tg(mpeg1:gal4);Tg(UAS:NTR-mCherry) triple-transgenic zebrafish shows that Mrc1a-eGFP(+) FGPs and Mpeg1-mCherry(+) macrophages are distinct cell populations (Figure 4o–t).
evidence: The claim is supported by triple-transgenic imaging data shown in Figure 4o-t (n = 5 animals imaged at 5 dpf, n = 3 animals imaged at 15 dpf).

claim: Lyve1-dsRed-positive perivascular cells do not overlap with Gfap:GFP-positive glial cells.
source: Finally, we compared the neuroanatomical location of Lyve1-dsRed-positive perivascular cells to the glial cell population labeled with a Tg(gfap:GFP) transgenic line and with the GFAP antibody using the Zebrafish Brain Browser software (Marquart et al., 2015), and found no overlap between the two cell populations. Glial cells are found throughout deep brain tissues but not on the brain surface, while as noted above, FGPs are located only in the most superficial exterior tissues, which are not Gfap:GFP-positive (Figure 4—figure supplement 1).
evidence: The claim is supported by analysis using the Zebrafish Brain Browser software (Marquart et al., 2015) shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1.

claim: Zebrafish FGPs are not neural crest derived based on lack of Sox10:dsRed expression.
source: To examine a potential neural crest contribution to FGP formation, we analyzed Tg(mrc1a:eGFP); Tg(sox10:dsRed) double transgenics at 3 dpf as FGPs begin to arise and at 5 dpf when they localize to the tectum and become sessile (Video 1, Figure 4—figure supplement 2). Time lapse imaging shows that 3 dpf emerging FGPs are Sox10:dsRed-negative (Video 1, Figure 4—figure supplement 2a,b), although Sox10:dsRed-positive pigment cells can be observed migrating on top of the Sox10:dsRed-negative FGPs (Video 1). FGPs also lack Sox10 expression at later stages, as shown by imaging FGPs on the 5 dpf optic tectum (Figure 4—figure supplement 2c–f). These results show that zebrafish FGPs are not neural crest derived.
evidence: The claim is supported by time-lapse and confocal imaging of double-transgenic animals shown in Video 1 and Figure 4—figure supplement 2 (n = 5 animals imaged).

claim: Knockdown of pu.1 does not affect FGP formation at 5 dpf.
source: To test whether FGPs are derived from primitive hematopoietic progenitors, we knocked down pu.1, a gene required for primitive hematopoiesis (Rhodes et al., 2005), in Tg(mrc1a:eGFP) embryos. As shown previously, pu.1 knockdown results in loss of expression of the granulocyte-specific marker myeloid-specific peroxidase (mpx) above the yolk and the intermediate cell mass (n = 15/15 embryos) at 20 hpf, confirming successful ablation of the primitive hematopoietic wave (Figure 5—figure supplement 1a–d). However, FGP numbers at 5 dpf are not significantly different from controls (Figure 5—figure supplement 1e–i), confirming that primitive hematopoiesis is not needed for FGP formation.
evidence: The claim is supported by morpholino knockdown experiments shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1 (t-test, p-value=0.76).

claim: Photoconversion of the dorsal aorta at 24 hpf does not result in red fluorescent FGPs at 5 dpf in Tg(egfl7:gal4);Tg(UAS:kaede);Tg(mrc1a:eGFP) triple transgenic animals.
source: We carefully photoconverted the entire dorsal aorta at 24 hpf and then examined Mrc1a:eGFP-positive FGPs for red fluorescence at 5 dpf. Animals in which the DA was photoconverted at 24 hpf had robust red fluorescence in the 5 dpf dorsal aorta (Figure 5e and Figure 5—figure supplement 2d,e) and in the thymus (Figure 5d and Figure 5—figure supplement 2f), but they had no red fluorescent FGPs in the 5 dpf brain (Figure 5f–h and Figure 5—figure supplement 2g,h; n(egfl7:gal4)=5/5; n(fli:gal4)=8/8;).
evidence: The claim is supported by photoconversion experiments shown in Figure 5f-h (n=5/5 photoconverted animals lacking red fluorescent FGPs).

claim: Photoconversion of the dorsal aorta at 24 hpf does not result in red fluorescent FGPs at 5 dpf in Tg(fli:gal4);Tg(UAS:kaede);Tg(mrc1a:eGFP) triple transgenic animals.
source: We carefully photoconverted the entire dorsal aorta at 24 hpf and then examined Mrc1a:eGFP-positive FGPs for red fluorescence at 5 dpf. Animals in which the DA was photoconverted at 24 hpf had robust red fluorescence in the 5 dpf dorsal aorta (Figure 5e and Figure 5—figure supplement 2d,e) and in the thymus (Figure 5d and Figure 5—figure supplement 2f), but they had no red fluorescent FGPs in the 5 dpf brain (Figure 5f–h and Figure 5—figure supplement 2g,h; n(egfl7:gal4)=5/5; n(fli:gal4)=8/8;).
evidence: The claim is supported by photoconversion experiments shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 2g,h (n=8/8 photoconverted animals lacking red fluorescent FGPs).

claim: Lyve1:dsRed-positive FGPs do not express Runx1:eGFP at 5 dpf.
source: To further rule out a potential hematopoietic ontogeny for zebrafish FGPs, we crossed the Tg(lyve1:dsRed) line to two different HSPC reporter lines, Tg(runx1:eGFP) and Tg(c-myb:eGFP) (North et al., 2007), and imaged the resulting Tg(lyve1:dsRed);Tg(runx1:eGFP) or Tg(lyve1:dsRed);Tg(c-myb:eGFP) double-transgenic animals at 5 dpf (Figure 5i–n). No Runx1:eGFP or c-Myb:eGFP expression was detected in Lyve1:DsRed-positive FGPs despite robust GFP expression in the thymus and/or in circulating GFP-positive monocytes (Figure 5i–n).
evidence: The claim is supported by double-transgenic imaging data shown in Figure 5i-l (n = 3 animals imaged).

claim: Lyve1:dsRed-positive FGPs do not express c-Myb:eGFP at 5 dpf.
source: To further rule out a potential hematopoietic ontogeny for zebrafish FGPs, we crossed the Tg(lyve1:dsRed) line to two different HSPC reporter lines, Tg(runx1:eGFP) and Tg(c-myb:eGFP) (North et al., 2007), and imaged the resulting Tg(lyve1:dsRed);Tg(runx1:eGFP) or Tg(lyve1:dsRed);Tg(c-myb:eGFP) double-transgenic animals at 5 dpf (Figure 5i–n). No Runx1:eGFP or c-Myb:eGFP expression was detected in Lyve1:DsRed-positive FGPs despite robust GFP expression in the thymus and/or in circulating GFP-positive monocytes (Figure 5i–n).
evidence: The claim is supported by double-transgenic imaging data shown in Figure 5m,n (n = 3 animals imaged).

claim: Runx1 knockdown significantly reduces Mpx:eGFP-positive cells at 5 dpf (t-test, p-value=0.012).
source: Finally, we decided to block the specification of HSPCs by knocking down runx1 (Gore et al., 2016) in Tg(lyve1:dsRed);Tg(mpx:eGFP) double transgenic embryos and examining them for the presence of FGPs. Inhibition of HSPC specification by runx1 knockdown led to a significant downregulation of Mpx-positive cells (Figure 5—figure supplement 3a–b',e; t-test, p-value=0.012), however, consistent with our previous observations, Lyve1-positive FGP formation and migration to the 5 dpf optic tectum was not affected (Figure 5—figure supplement 3c–d,f, t-test, p-value=0.22).
evidence: The claim is supported by morpholino knockdown experiments with statistical analysis shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 3 (n = 4 animals imaged and quantitated).

claim: Runx1 knockdown does not affect Lyve1-positive FGP formation and migration to the 5 dpf optic tectum (t-test, p-value=0.22).
source: Finally, we decided to block the specification of HSPCs by knocking down runx1 (Gore et al., 2016) in Tg(lyve1:dsRed);Tg(mpx:eGFP) double transgenic embryos and examining them for the presence of FGPs. Inhibition of HSPC specification by runx1 knockdown led to a significant downregulation of Mpx-positive cells (Figure 5—figure supplement 3a–b',e; t-test, p-value=0.012), however, consistent with our previous observations, Lyve1-positive FGP formation and migration to the 5 dpf optic tectum was not affected (Figure 5—figure supplement 3c–d,f, t-test, p-value=0.22).
evidence: The claim is supported by morpholino knockdown experiments with statistical analysis shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 3 (n = 8 animals imaged and quantitated).

claim: FGPs express high levels of lympho-venous endothelial markers such as mrc1a, lyve1b, stab1, stab2 and prox1a compared to whole fish.
source: In comparison to the whole fish, FGPs express high levels of lympho-venous endothelial markers such as mrc1a, lyve1b, stab1, stab2 and prox1a, as well as the lymphangiogenic ligand vegfd (Figure 6c).
evidence: The claim is supported by RNA-seq analysis of FACS-sorted FGPs shown in Figure 6c.

claim: FGPs express high levels of the lymphangiogenic ligand vegfd compared to whole fish.
source: In comparison to the whole fish, FGPs express high levels of lympho-venous endothelial markers such as mrc1a, lyve1b, stab1, stab2 and prox1a, as well as the lymphangiogenic ligand vegfd (Figure 6c).
evidence: The claim is supported by RNA-seq analysis of FACS-sorted FGPs shown in Figure 6c.

claim: FGPs show significantly lower expression of pecam1 endothelial cell-cell adhesion protein compared to whole fish.
source: However, FGPs show significantly lower expression of some key blood endothelial markers, including the pecam1 endothelial cell-cell adhesion protein, and the pro-angiogenic ligand vegfaa, compared to either the whole fish (Figure 6c), or especially mCherry-positive blood endothelial cells, where the zebrafish vegfr2 receptor kdrl expression is also significantly low (Figure 6—figure supplement 1a).
evidence: The claim is supported by RNA-seq analysis of FACS-sorted FGPs shown in Figure 6c.

claim: FGPs show significantly lower expression of the pro-angiogenic ligand vegfaa compared to whole fish.
source: However, FGPs show significantly lower expression of some key blood endothelial markers, including the pecam1 endothelial cell-cell adhesion protein, and the pro-angiogenic ligand vegfaa, compared to either the whole fish (Figure 6c), or especially mCherry-positive blood endothelial cells, where the zebrafish vegfr2 receptor kdrl expression is also significantly low (Figure 6—figure supplement 1a).
evidence: The claim is supported by RNA-seq analysis of FACS-sorted FGPs shown in Figure 6c.

claim: FGPs show significantly lower expression of kdrl (vegfr2 receptor) compared to mCherry-positive blood endothelial cells.
source: However, FGPs show significantly lower expression of some key blood endothelial markers, including the pecam1 endothelial cell-cell adhesion protein, and the pro-angiogenic ligand vegfaa, compared to either the whole fish (Figure 6c), or especially mCherry-positive blood endothelial cells, where the zebrafish vegfr2 receptor kdrl expression is also significantly low (Figure 6—figure supplement 1a).
evidence: The claim is supported by RNA-seq analysis comparing FGPs to blood endothelial cells shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 1a.

claim: FGPs express reduced levels of macrophage markers compared to whole fish.
source: Comparison between FGPs and whole fish RNA-seq profiles also confirmed that FGPs express reduced levels of macrophage markers (Figure 6d), astrocyte/glial markers (Figure 6e), neurotrophic factors (Figure 6e), and pericyte markers (Figure 6f).
evidence: The claim is supported by RNA-seq analysis shown in Figure 6d.

claim: FGPs express reduced levels of astrocyte/glial markers compared to whole fish.
source: Comparison between FGPs and whole fish RNA-seq profiles also confirmed that FGPs express reduced levels of macrophage markers (Figure 6d), astrocyte/glial markers (Figure 6e), neurotrophic factors (Figure 6e), and pericyte markers (Figure 6f).
evidence: The claim is supported by RNA-seq analysis shown in Figure 6e.

claim: FGPs express reduced levels of neurotrophic factors compared to whole fish.
source: Comparison between FGPs and whole fish RNA-seq profiles also confirmed that FGPs express reduced levels of macrophage markers (Figure 6d), astrocyte/glial markers (Figure 6e), neurotrophic factors (Figure 6e), and pericyte markers (Figure 6f).
evidence: The claim is supported by RNA-seq analysis shown in Figure 6e.

claim: FGPs express reduced levels of pericyte markers compared to whole fish.
source: Comparison between FGPs and whole fish RNA-seq profiles also confirmed that FGPs express reduced levels of macrophage markers (Figure 6d), astrocyte/glial markers (Figure 6e), neurotrophic factors (Figure 6e), and pericyte markers (Figure 6f).
evidence: The claim is supported by RNA-seq analysis shown in Figure 6f.

claim: FGPs express higher levels of some pro-angiogenic ligands than blood endothelial cells, including vegfab, egfl7, and the receptors tie1 and flt4 (vefgr3).
source: Interestingly, FGPs express higher levels of some pro-angiogenic ligands than blood endothelial cells, including vegfab, egfl7, and the receptors tie1 and flt4 (vefgr3) (Figure 6—figure supplement 1a).
evidence: The claim is supported by RNA-seq analysis comparing FGPs to blood endothelial cells shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 1a.

claim: At 3 dpf FGPs are present in low numbers in more lateral positions in the head.
source: To determine the origins of FGPs, we examined the earliest stages of emergence of these cells during development using Tg(mrc1a:eGFP);Tg(kdrl:mCherry) double-transgenic animals. At 3 dpf FGPs are present in low numbers in more lateral positions in the head (Figure 7a–c, Figure 7—figure supplement 1a,b), but by 4 dpf these cells are present in larger numbers in more dorsal and medial parts of the brain, especially the surface of the optic tectum (Figure 7d,e, Figure 7—figure supplement 1c,d), suggesting the cells may migrate dorso-medially to the tectum.
evidence: The claim is supported by developmental time-course imaging shown in Figure 7a-c.

claim: By 4 dpf FGPs are present in larger numbers in more dorsal and medial parts of the brain, especially the surface of the optic tectum.
source: To determine the origins of FGPs, we examined the earliest stages of emergence of these cells during development using Tg(mrc1a:eGFP);Tg(kdrl:mCherry) double-transgenic animals. At 3 dpf FGPs are present in low numbers in more lateral positions in the head (Figure 7a–c, Figure 7—figure supplement 1a,b), but by 4 dpf these cells are present in larger numbers in more dorsal and medial parts of the brain, especially the surface of the optic tectum (Figure 7d,e, Figure 7—figure supplement 1c,d), suggesting the cells may migrate dorso-medially to the tectum.
evidence: The claim is supported by developmental time-course imaging shown in Figure 7d,e.

claim: FGP progenitors emerge from deep lateral regions on either side of the head behind the eye, migrating dorsally and then medially to the optic tectum along newly-formed blood vessels.
source: Confocal time-lapse imaging of Tg(mrc1a:eGFP); Tg(kdrl:mCherry) larvae confirmed that FGP progenitors emerge from deep lateral regions on either side of the head behind the eye, migrating dorsally and then medially to the optic tectum along newly-formed blood vessels (Figure 7f–j, Video 2).
evidence: The claim is supported by time-lapse confocal imaging shown in Figure 7f-j and Video 2.

claim: Migratory FGPs are polarized and possess highly active protrusions.
source: Migratory FGPs are polarized and possess highly active protrusions (Figure 7f–j,).
evidence: The claim is supported by time-lapse imaging shown in Figure 7f-j.

claim: Once FGPs reach the optic tectum, they lose their migratory behavior and become sessile.
source: Interestingly, once FGPs reach the optic tectum, they lose their migratory behavior and become sessile, although they appear to maintain some protrusive behavior throughout life.
evidence: The claim is based on observations from time-lapse imaging experiments.

claim: FGPs emerge from the optic choroidal vascular plexus (OCVP).
source: We performed additional time-lapse imaging experiments focusing on the region behind the eye from which FGPs appeared to be emerging. Although visualization of the deep cranial regions behind the eye is challenging, time-lapse imaging in Tg(mrc1a:eGFP);Tg(kdrl:mCherry) animals shows that FGPs emerge from the optic choroidal vascular plexus (OCVP), a network of vessels that forms adjacent to the pigment epithelium on the deep medial surface of the eye (Figure 7a, Video 3 and 4).
evidence: The claim is supported by time-lapse imaging shown in Figure 7a and Videos 3 and 4.

claim: FGPs delaminate from the OCVP and begin to express high levels of Mrc1a:eGFP, eventually migrating away from the OCVP along Kdrl:mCherry-positive vessels.
source: FGPs delaminate from the OCVP and begin to express high levels of Mrc1a:eGFP, eventually migrating away from the OCVP, generally along Kdrl:mCherry-positive vessels (Figure 7f–j).
evidence: The claim is supported by time-lapse imaging shown in Figure 7f-j.

claim: Photoconversion of the OCVP at 2.5 dpf results in red fluorescent labeling of FGPs on the optic tectum at 4-5 dpf in Tg(egfl7:gal4);Tg(UAS:kaede);Tg(mrc1a:eGFP) triple-transgenic animals (1.25 ± 1.14 S.D. FGPs per tectal neuropile, n = 12 embryos).
source: Photoconversion of the OCVP was carried out at 2.5 dpf, before FGP emergence, and the animals were scored for the presence of red fluorescence in FGPs on the optic tectum at 4–5 dpf. Unlike photoconversion of the dorsal aorta, which did not result in any red fluorescent labeling of brain FGPs, photoconversion of the OCVP led to red fluorescent labeling of FGPs in both triple-transgenic lines (egfl7:gal4 line: 1.25 ± 1.14 S.D. FGPs per tectal neuropile, n = 12 embryos; fli:gal4 line = 1.37 ± 1.98 S.D. FGPs per tectal neuropile, n = 19 embryos), together with some adjacent blood vessels that grew dorsally as well (Figure 7o–r, Figure 7—figure supplement 2b–e).
evidence: The claim is supported by photoconversion experiments shown in Figure 7o-r (n = 8/12 embryos showed Red Kaede).

claim: Photoconversion of the OCVP at 2.5 dpf results in red fluorescent labeling of FGPs on the optic tectum at 4-5 dpf in Tg(fli:gal4);Tg(UAS:kaede);Tg(mrc1a:eGFP) triple-transgenic animals (1.37 ± 1.98 S.D. FGPs per tectal neuropile, n = 19 embryos).
source: Photoconversion of the OCVP was carried out at 2.5 dpf, before FGP emergence, and the animals were scored for the presence of red fluorescence in FGPs on the optic tectum at 4–5 dpf. Unlike photoconversion of the dorsal aorta, which did not result in any red fluorescent labeling of brain FGPs, photoconversion of the OCVP led to red fluorescent labeling of FGPs in both triple-transgenic lines (egfl7:gal4 line: 1.25 ± 1.14 S.D. FGPs per tectal neuropile, n = 12 embryos; fli:gal4 line = 1.37 ± 1.98 S.D. FGPs per tectal neuropile, n = 19 embryos), together with some adjacent blood vessels that grew dorsally as well (Figure 7o–r, Figure 7—figure supplement 2b–e).
evidence: The claim is supported by photoconversion experiments shown in Figure 7—figure supplement 2b-e (n = 9/19 embryos showed Red Kaede).

claim: Nascent FGPs are weakly Kdrl:mCherry positive as they emerge from the OCVP, but this red fluorescence diminishes and is lost as the cells migrate away.
source: Time lapse imaging of FGPs emerging from the OCVP in Tg(mrc1a:eGFP);Tg(kdrl:mCherry) animals shows that nascent FGPs are weakly Kdrl:mCherry positive, as might be expected of cells differentiating from primitive endothelium (Figure 8a–g, Video 5), however this red fluorescence diminishes and is lost as the cells migrate away from the OCVP.
evidence: The claim is supported by time-lapse imaging shown in Figure 8a-g and Video 5.

claim: Kdrl:nlsmCherry-positive FGPs are readily observed migrating out from the OCVP in Tg(mrc1a:eGFP);Tg(kdrl:nlsmCherry) animals.
source: We were able to visualize Kdrl-positive emerging FGPs even more clearly by performing time-lapse imaging of the OCVP in Tg(mrc1a:eGFP);Tg(kdrl:nlsmCherry) animals with red fluorescent endothelial nuclei (Figure 8h–k, Video 6), where Kdrl:nlsmCherry-positive FGPs were readily observed migrating out from the OCVP.
evidence: The claim is supported by time-lapse imaging shown in Figure 8h-k and Video 6.

claim: EGFP-positive FGPs are present in Tg(kdrl:Cre)s898;Tg(-9.8actb2:LOXP-DsRed-LOXP-EGFP)s928 double transgenic 'switch' line at 4 dpf.
source: The endothelial origin of FGPs was further confirmed using a Tg(kdrl:Cre)s898;Tg(-9.8actb2:LOXP-DsRed-LOXP-EGFP)s928 (Kikuchi et al., 2010) double transgenic 'switch' line (Figure 9a–c). In this double transgenic line, non-endothelial tissues are all dsRed-positive and EGFP-negative, but a small percentage of endothelial cells mosaically become EGFP-positive (Cre expression in the Kdrl:Cre line is not sufficient to switch EGFP on in all endothelial cells). As expected, EGFP-positive blood vessels were observed in the double-transgenic line at 5 dpf (Figure 9d, Figure 9—figure supplement 1a–b), although only a minor subset of endothelial cells were 'switched' to red fluorescence, as seen clearly by comparing with complete vessel labeling in a Tg(kdrl:mCherry) embryo (Figure 9—figure supplement 1c). Using Qdot705 angiography to mark developing brain blood vessels in 4 dpf animals, we also observed a subset of EGFP-positive FGPs adjacent to these vessels (Figure 9d,e).
evidence: The claim is supported by imaging of the double transgenic 'switch' line shown in Figure 9d,e.

claim: EGFP-positive FGPs are present on the brains of Tg(kdrl:Cre)s898;Tg(-9.8actb2:LOXP-DsRed-LOXP-EGFP)s928 double transgenic adult animals.
source: As similar small proportion of EGFP-positive blood vessel endothelial cells and EGFP-positive FGPs were observed on the brains of Tg(kdrl:Cre)s898;Tg(-9.8actb2:LOXP-DsRed-LOXP-EGFP)s928 double transgenic adult animals (Figure 9f–i, Figure 9—figure supplement 1d–f).
evidence: The claim is supported by imaging of adult double transgenic 'switch' animals shown in Figure 9f-i.

claim: The presence of EGFP-positive FGPs in the Kdrl:Cre transgenic switch line confirms that FGPs emerge from Kdrl-positive progenitors early in development.
source: The presence of EGFP-positive FGPs in this transgenic switch line confirms the idea that FGPs emerge from Kdrl-positive progenitors early in development.
evidence: The claim is an inference based on the observation of EGFP-positive FGPs in the Kdrl:Cre switch line.

claim: Zebrafish brain FGPs have a primitive venous endothelial origin.
source: Together, these and our other results suggest that zebrafish brain FGPs have a primitive venous endothelial origin.
evidence: This is a summary claim integrating multiple lines of evidence from the study.

claim: The blood-brain barrier is essential for the proper homeostasis and function of the CNS.
source: The blood-brain barrier is essential for the proper homeostasis and function of the CNS, but its mechanism of function is poorly understood.
evidence: This is a statement of established scientific knowledge.

claim: Perivascular cells surrounding brain blood vessels are thought to be important for blood-brain barrier establishment.
source: Perivascular cells surrounding brain blood vessels are thought to be important for blood-brain barrier establishment, but their roles are not well defined.
evidence: This is a statement of current scientific understanding.

claim: Zebrafish FGPs appear to be the zebrafish equivalent of cells variably characterized as Fluorescent Granular Perithelial cells (FGPs), perivascular macrophages, or 'Mato Cells' in mammals based on similarities in morphology, location, and scavenger behavior.
source: Based on similarities in their morphology, location, and scavenger behavior, these cells appear to be the zebrafish equivalent of cells variably characterized as Fluorescent Granular Perithelial cells (FGPs), perivascular macrophages, or 'Mato Cells' in mammals.
evidence: This is an inference based on comparative analysis of zebrafish and mammalian cells.

claim: Zebrafish FGPs appear molecularly most similar to lymphatic endothelium.
source: Despite their macrophage-like morphology and perivascular location, zebrafish FGPs appear molecularly most similar to lymphatic endothelium, and our imaging studies suggest that these cells emerge by differentiation from endothelium of the optic choroidal vascular plexus.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on RNA-seq analysis and transgene expression patterns.

claim: This is the first report of a perivascular cell population in the brain derived from vascular endothelium.
source: Our findings provide the first report of a perivascular cell population in the brain derived from vascular endothelium.
evidence: This is a claim about the novelty of the findings.

claim: The Prox1 gene is regarded as a lymphatic 'master regulator' based on studies in mouse, zebrafish, Xenopus and chick.
source: The Prox1 gene is regarded as a lymphatic 'master regulator' based on a series of studies performed in mouse, zebrafish, Xenopus and chick (Hong et al., 2002; Oliver and Harvey, 2002; Peyrot et al., 2010; Rodriguez-Niedenführ et al., 2001; Wigle et al., 2002; Wigle and Oliver, 1999; Yaniv et al., 2006).
evidence: This is a statement of established scientific knowledge supported by multiple citations.

claim: Mouse dural sinuses host functional lymphatic vessels capable of performing conventional lymphatic functions.
source: Although it had been accepted that lymphatic vessels and related organs are found in every tissue of the body with the exclusive exception of the bone marrow and the CNS, a recent study showed that mouse dural sinuses host functional lymphatic vessels capable of performing conventional lymphatic functions (Louveau et al., 2015).
evidence: This is a statement of recent findings from another study.

claim: CNS-associated lymphatic vessels express classic lymphatic markers such as Lyve1 and Prox1.
source: These CNS-associated lymphatic vessels express classic lymphatic markers such as Lyve1 and Prox1 but it is unclear whether these vessels actually form from preexisting veins like lymphatic vessels elsewhere in the body (Louveau et al., 2015).
evidence: This is a statement of findings from another study.

claim: Under homeostatic conditions, the BBB is responsible for protecting the brain from the entry of pathogens, neurotoxic molecules and lipophilic elements.
source: Under homeostatic conditions, the BBB is responsible for protecting the brain from the entry of pathogens, neurotoxic molecules and lipophilic elements (Ballabh et al., 2004).
evidence: This is a statement of established scientific knowledge.

claim: CNS-associated endothelial cells and specialized CNS perivascular cells including astrocytes, pericytes, microglia, and perivascular macrophages are thought to be important for BBB function in the brain.
source: CNS-associated endothelial cells and a variety of specialized CNS perivascular cells including astrocytes, pericytes, microglia, and perivascular macrophages (PVMs) are thought to be important for BBB function in the brain (Williams et al., 2001).
evidence: This is a statement of current scientific understanding.

claim: PVMs appear to be important for protecting the brain from toxic or potentially damaging elements such as lipids, heavy metals, and complex sugars based on their known scavenging properties.
source: Based on their known scavenging properties, PVMs appear to be important for protecting the brain from toxic or potentially damaging elements such as lipids, heavy metals, and complex sugars, among others (Linehan et al., 2000; Mato et al., 1997, 1982b, 1984, 2002; Mendes-Jorge et al., 2009).
evidence: This is an inference based on known properties of PVMs from cited studies.

claim: Clodronate-dependent ablation of PVMs in the mouse showed that PVMs help suppress vascular permeability and maintain the integrity of the blood vascular barrier at baseline.
source: Clodronate-dependent ablation of PVMs in the mouse showed that at base line, PVMs help suppress vascular permeability and maintain the integrity of the blood vascular barrier, and when VEGF was added in combination with PVM ablation, vessel leakage increased significantly (He et al., 2016).
evidence: This is a statement of findings from another study.

claim: When VEGF was added in combination with PVM ablation, vessel leakage increased significantly.
source: Clodronate-dependent ablation of PVMs in the mouse showed that at base line, PVMs help suppress vascular permeability and maintain the integrity of the blood vascular barrier, and when VEGF was added in combination with PVM ablation, vessel leakage increased significantly (He et al., 2016).
evidence: This is a statement of findings from another study.

claim: Saturated fatty acids found on high fat diets reduce Glucose Receptor 1 (GLUT1) expression in the BBB of mice, impeding brain glucose uptake.
source: On the metabolic side, another recent study showed that the saturated fatty acids found on high fat diets reduce Glucose Receptor 1 (GLUT1) expression in the BBB of mice, impeding brain glucose uptake, but this life threatening effect is ameliorated by the production of VEGF by myeloid-derived PVMs, driving the upregulation of GLUT1 back to homeostatic levels (Jais et al., 2016).
evidence: This is a statement of findings from another study.

claim: The life threatening effect of reduced GLUT1 expression is ameliorated by the production of VEGF by myeloid-derived PVMs, driving the upregulation of GLUT1 back to homeostatic levels.
source: On the metabolic side, another recent study showed that the saturated fatty acids found on high fat diets reduce Glucose Receptor 1 (GLUT1) expression in the BBB of mice, impeding brain glucose uptake, but this life threatening effect is ameliorated by the production of VEGF by myeloid-derived PVMs, driving the upregulation of GLUT1 back to homeostatic levels (Jais et al., 2016).
evidence: This is a statement of findings from another study.

claim: Brain perivascular cells called 'Fluorescent Granular Perithelial Cells' (FGPs) were first identified as a result of their yellow fluorescence due to the accumulation of intracellular vesicles containing autofluorescent lipid breakdown products.
source: Brain perivascular cells called 'Fluorescent Granular Perithelial Cells' (FGPs) were first identified as a result of their yellow fluorescence due to the accumulation of intracellular vesicles containing autofluorescent lipid breakdown products (Mato et al., 1981).
evidence: This is a statement of historical findings from cited literature.

claim: FGPs are found in the leptomeningeal layers and cerebral cortex of mammals.
source: FGPs are found in the leptomeningeal layers and cerebral cortex of mammals, where they are thought to provide an important pinocytotic protective function, leading to encapsulation of particles within the cells and giving them their stereotypical 'honeycomb like' morphology in light and electron micrographs (Mato et al., 1986a, 2002).
evidence: This is a statement of established knowledge from cited literature.

claim: FGPs are thought to provide an important pinocytotic protective function, leading to encapsulation of particles within the cells.
source: FGPs are found in the leptomeningeal layers and cerebral cortex of mammals, where they are thought to provide an important pinocytotic protective function, leading to encapsulation of particles within the cells and giving them their stereotypical 'honeycomb like' morphology in light and electron micrographs (Mato et al., 1986a, 2002).
evidence: This is a statement of proposed function from cited literature.

claim: The internal vesicles present in FGPs increase with age.
source: The internal vesicles present in FGPs increase with age, and studies have correlated increased FGP vesicle accumulation with onset of cognitive neurological impairment in conditions such as Alzheimer's disease and in lipid metabolic disorders (Mato and Ookawara, 1981; Mato et al., 1981, 1982a).
evidence: This is a statement of findings from cited literature.

claim: Studies have correlated increased FGP vesicle accumulation with onset of cognitive neurological impairment in conditions such as Alzheimer's disease and in lipid metabolic disorders.
source: The internal vesicles present in FGPs increase with age, and studies have correlated increased FGP vesicle accumulation with onset of cognitive neurological impairment in conditions such as Alzheimer's disease and in lipid metabolic disorders (Mato and Ookawara, 1981; Mato et al., 1981, 1982a).
evidence: This is a statement of correlations found in cited literature.

claim: Several studies in mammals have suggested that PVMs and/or FGPs are bone marrow-derived cells.
source: Several studies in mammals have suggested that PVMs and/or FGPs are bone marrow-derived cells (Audoy-Rémus et al., 2008; Faraco et al., 2016).
evidence: This is a statement of findings from cited literature.

claim: PVMs are thought to form when mature monocytes extravasate from brain vessels in response to pro-inflammatory cytokines.
source: Specifically, PVMs are thought to form when mature monocytes extravasate from brain vessels in response to pro-inflammatory cytokines (Audoy-Rémus et al., 2008).
evidence: This is a statement of proposed mechanism from cited literature.

claim: PVMs strongly express CD206 (aka Mannose Receptor 1, MRC1), a receptor commonly expressed by tissue resident macrophages required to mediate endocytosis of glycoproteins.
source: The fact that PVMs strongly express CD206 (aka Mannose Receptor 1, MRC1), a receptor commonly expressed by tissue resident macrophages required to mediate endocytosis of glycoproteins (Apostolopoulos and McKenzie, 2001; Faraco et al., 2016; Linehan et al., 2000), has also been taken as an indication of a macrophage identity for these cells.
evidence: This is a statement of known molecular characteristics from cited literature.

claim: CD206(+) PVM levels increase during a high fat diet.
source: As noted above, CD206(+) PVM levels increase during a high fat diet and PVMs restore the balance of brain glucose uptake by secreting VEGFA.
evidence: This is a statement of findings from cited literature.

claim: PVMs restore the balance of brain glucose uptake by secreting VEGFA during high fat diet.
source: As noted above, CD206(+) PVM levels increase during a high fat diet and PVMs restore the balance of brain glucose uptake by secreting VEGFA.
evidence: This is a statement of findings from cited literature.

claim: VEGF myeloid-specific deletion (using a Lys:Cre mouse) produced by CD206-positive cells during high fat diet feeding leads to failure in glucose uptake.
source: VEGF myeloid-specific deletion (using a Lys:Cre mouse) produced by CD206-positive cells during high fat diet feeding leads to failure in glucose uptake, consistent with a hematopoietic origin for these cells (Jais et al., 2016).
evidence: This is a statement of findings from cited literature.

claim: Mannose Receptors recognize complex sugars on the surface of pathogens, facilitating phagocytic engulfment and neutralization of viruses, bacteria and fungi.
source: Mannose Receptors recognize complex sugars on the surface of pathogens, facilitating phagocytic engulfment and neutralization of viruses, bacteria and fungi (Apostolopoulos and McKenzie, 2001; Gazi and Martinez-Pomares, 2009; Linehan et al., 2000; Op den Brouw et al., 2009; Sweet et al., 2010).
evidence: This is a statement of established molecular function from cited literature.

claim: PVMs play an important role in recruiting neutrophils to infection/injury sites by secreting a battery of chemokines.
source: A recent study in which murine ear skin was inoculated with Staphylococcus aureus also showed that PVMs play an important role in recruiting neutrophils to the infection/injury site by secreting a battery of chemokines (Abtin et al., 2014).
evidence: This is a statement of findings from cited literature.

claim: PVMs have been described in the brain cerebral cortex, retina, skin, peritoneum, mesentery and cremaster muscle.
source: However, it is interesting to note that while PVMs have been described in the brain cerebral cortex, as well as in the retina, skin, peritoneum, mesentery and cremaster muscle (Abtin et al., 2014; He et al., 2016; Jais et al., 2016; Mendes-Jorge et al., 2009), FGPs with their highly characteristic autofluorescent vesicles have only been described in the mammalian brain and in the retina (Mato et al., 1981; Mendes-Jorge et al., 2009), suggesting that FGPs may be different from or define a subset of PVM cells.
evidence: This is a statement of findings from cited literature.

claim: FGPs with their highly characteristic autofluorescent vesicles have only been described in the mammalian brain and in the retina.
source: However, it is interesting to note that while PVMs have been described in the brain cerebral cortex, as well as in the retina, skin, peritoneum, mesentery and cremaster muscle (Abtin et al., 2014; He et al., 2016; Jais et al., 2016; Mendes-Jorge et al., 2009), FGPs with their highly characteristic autofluorescent vesicles have only been described in the mammalian brain and in the retina (Mato et al., 1981; Mendes-Jorge et al., 2009), suggesting that FGPs may be different from or define a subset of PVM cells.
evidence: This is a statement of findings from cited literature with an inference.

claim: FGPs may be different from or define a subset of PVM cells.
source: However, it is interesting to note that while PVMs have been described in the brain cerebral cortex, as well as in the retina, skin, peritoneum, mesentery and cremaster muscle (Abtin et al., 2014; He et al., 2016; Jais et al., 2016; Mendes-Jorge et al., 2009), FGPs with their highly characteristic autofluorescent vesicles have only been described in the mammalian brain and in the retina (Mato et al., 1981; Mendes-Jorge et al., 2009), suggesting that FGPs may be different from or define a subset of PVM cells.
evidence: This is a speculative inference based on the distribution of FGPs versus PVMs.

claim: In the mammalian cerebral cortex, FGPs and microglia are separate cell populations based on their time of appearance, anatomical location, morphology and capacity to take up Horseradish Peroxidase.
source: Mrc1a-positive cells are not microglia based on our Neutral Red staining (Figure 4d,e), a result supported by findings of previous studies in rats where both cell populations where clearly separated by their time of appearance, anatomical location, morphology and capacity to take up Horseradish Peroxidase (Mato et al., 1985).
evidence: This is a statement of findings from cited literature.

claim: In human brain samples from individuals suffering from neurodegeneration, lymphomas, sarcomas and brain hemorrhages, the marker GP-3 specifically labels FGPs and not macrophages or microglia.
source: Furthermore, in human brain samples from individuals suffering from neurodegeneration, lymphomas, sarcomas and brain hemorrhages, the marker GP-3 was found to specifically label FGPs and not macrophages or microglia under these immune compromised conditions (Yokoo et al., 2000).
evidence: This is a statement of findings from cited literature.

claim: Pericytes and FGPs are separate cell populations in rat cerebrums based on location and distribution.
source: Similarly, pericytes and FGPs were also described as separate cell populations in rat cerebrums, again based on location and distribution (Ookawara et al., 1996).
evidence: This is a statement of findings from cited literature.

claim: FGPs and pericytes are morphologically distinct in electron micrographs, with FGPs appearing swollen and loaded full of granules, whereas pericytes are flat.
source: These cells are also morphologically distinct in electron micrographs, with FGPs appearing swollen and loaded full of granules, whereas pericytes were flat (Ookawara et al., 1996).
evidence: This is a statement of findings from cited literature.

claim: During definitive hematopoiesis, HSPCs emerge from endothelial cells on the ventral side of the dorsal aorta beginning at approximately 24–26 hpf.
source: During definitive hematopoiesis, HSPCs emerge from endothelial cells on the ventral side of the dorsal aorta beginning at approximately 24–26 hpf (Boisset et al., 2010; Gérard et al., 2010; Gore et al., 2016; Kissa and Herbomel, 2010; Murayama et al., 2006) (Figure 5a).
evidence: This is a statement of established knowledge from cited literature.

claim: Definitive HSPCs migrate to sites of hematopoiesis such as the thymus and anterior kidney, where they differentiate to give rise to downstream blood lineages.
source: Definitive HSPCs migrate to sites of hematopoiesis such as the thymus and anterior kidney, where they differentiate to give rise to downstream blood lineages (Kissa and Herbomel, 2010; Murayama et al., 2006).
evidence: This is a statement of established knowledge from cited literature.

claim: The kdrl gene encodes a highly vascular endothelial-specific transcription factor.
source: The kdrl gene encodes a highly vascular endothelial-specific transcription factor (Covassin et al., 2006), and the Kdrl:nlsmCherry and Kdrl:Cre transgenes are expressed exclusively in endothelial cells, so the transient appearance of Kdrl:mCherry in FGP nuclei as they emerge from the optic choroidal vascular plexus and permanent marking of FGPs in the Kdrl:Cre background provides additional strong evidence that these cells are transdifferentiating from blood vascular endothelium.
evidence: This is a statement of established knowledge from cited literature.

claim: The Kdrl:nlsmCherry and Kdrl:Cre transgenes are expressed exclusively in endothelial cells.
source: The kdrl gene encodes a highly vascular endothelial-specific transcription factor (Covassin et al., 2006), and the Kdrl:nlsmCherry and Kdrl:Cre transgenes are expressed exclusively in endothelial cells, so the transient appearance of Kdrl:mCherry in FGP nuclei as they emerge from the optic choroidal vascular plexus and permanent marking of FGPs in the Kdrl:Cre background provides additional strong evidence that these cells are transdifferentiating from blood vascular endothelium.
evidence: This is a statement about transgene specificity.

claim: The transient appearance of Kdrl:mCherry in FGP nuclei as they emerge from the optic choroidal vascular plexus and permanent marking of FGPs in the Kdrl:Cre background provides strong evidence that these cells are transdifferentiating from blood vascular endothelium.
source: The kdrl gene encodes a highly vascular endothelial-specific transcription factor (Covassin et al., 2006), and the Kdrl:nlsmCherry and Kdrl:Cre transgenes are expressed exclusively in endothelial cells, so the transient appearance of Kdrl:mCherry in FGP nuclei as they emerge from the optic choroidal vascular plexus and permanent marking of FGPs in the Kdrl:Cre background provides additional strong evidence that these cells are transdifferentiating from blood vascular endothelium.
evidence: This is an inference based on the transgene expression patterns observed.

claim: HSPCs rapidly lose endothelial identity after emerging from the dorsal aorta.
source: It is worth noting that while HSPCs rapidly lose endothelial identity after emerging from the dorsal aorta, FGPs maintain a gene expression signature of lympho-venous identity indefinitely.
evidence: This is a statement of established knowledge about HSPC differentiation.

claim: FGPs maintain a gene expression signature of lympho-venous identity indefinitely.
source: It is worth noting that while HSPCs rapidly lose endothelial identity after emerging from the dorsal aorta, FGPs maintain a gene expression signature of lympho-venous identity indefinitely.
evidence: This is an inference based on the RNA-seq data and transgene expression patterns observed in adult FGPs.
